nameStory: The Saddled Prominent gets its name from the distinctive saddle-shaped marking across its back when at rest. Like a horse's saddle, this dark band stretches across the moth's folded wings, creating an unmistakable profile that makes identification easy even from a distance.
description: The Saddled Prominent is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches across. It belongs to the prominent moth family, known for their habit of raising their abdomens when disturbed, creating a prominent silhouette. The moth has mottled brown and gray wings with intricate patterns that help it blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. Its most striking feature is the dark saddle-like band that gives it its common name.

idTips.label: Saddle marking
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive dark brown or black band that stretches across the wings when the moth is at rest, resembling a horse's saddle

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings feel delicately scaled and have a soft, almost fuzzy appearance with intricate wavy lines and mottled patterns in browns and grays

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: At rest, holds wings tent-like over its body and may raise its abdomen in a defensive prominent posture when disturbed

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: About the size of a large postage stamp when wings are spread, noticeably bigger than most common house moths

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Males have feathery, brush-like antennae that feel soft to the touch, while females have thinner, thread-like antennae

habitat: Saddled Prominents are found in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where oak, maple, and birch trees are abundant. They prefer mature woodlands and forest edges rather than open fields, as their caterpillars feed on the leaves of various hardwood trees. You'll most likely encounter them near outdoor lights in wooded areas or resting on tree bark during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, typically May, as temperatures warm. Look for them at porch lights and moth sheets during mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs from June through August. Adults are most active on warm, humid nights and are attracted to artificial lights. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: A second generation may appear in early fall, though numbers are typically lower. Look for fresh adults in September in southern New England.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in soil or leaf litter. No adult moths are active during winter months.

funFact: When threatened, Saddled Prominent caterpillars can actually shoot their own feces up to several feet away as a defense mechanism, earning them the nickname "explosive caterpillars" among some moth enthusiasts!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other prominent moths, but the saddle marking is quite distinctive. If you can't see the saddle clearly, remember that Saddled Prominents tend to be more grayish-brown overall, while many similar species lean more toward reddish-brown or have more contrasting white markings.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "prominent" moths, this refers to their defensive posture of raising their abdomen, not their abundance or size. Many people assume prominent moths are rare or large, but they're actually fairly common and medium-sized members of New England's moth fauna.
compareHints: As the only Cecrita species in New England, compare it to other prominent moths like the White-dotted Prominent or Variable Oakleaf Caterpillar Moth. The Saddled Prominent is distinguished by its cleaner saddle marking and less contrasting wing patterns. Unlike the White-dotted Prominent, it lacks prominent white spots, and unlike the Variable Oakleaf moth, it has more subdued coloration overall.
